title: Shakespeare's theater
subject: art
description: In London, Shakespeare wrote for the Globe. Hamlet, Macbeth, Romeo: popular theater that has become the pinnacle of the English language.

hero.hook: An actor's playwright, a theater without sets... and eternal lines.

blocks.text: **William Shakespeare** (1564-1616) wrote for the London stage, not for the school. His plays mix kings, clowns, lovers and assassins.
Four centuries later, it is still played everywhere.
With the [[Lord Chamberlain's Men]] troupe, he plays, an open-air circle. The [[Globe Theater]] pay little and stay standing near the stage. The theater is popular, noisy, lively. [[Groundlings]]
Elizabethan London loves spectacle. Theaters compete with sermons and bear fights. Shakespeare writes in this noisy market, not in an ivory tower.

blocks.caption: The Globe: the scene pushed into the crowd.

blocks.text: He often writes in Shakespearean blank verse: iambic pentameter without rhyme. Insults, poems, monologues: he invents words and establishes characters (Hamlet, Lady Macbeth) who have become myths.
He recycles chronicles, Italian news, old pieces. The originality is in the language and the characters, not in the pure invention of the plot.
Several of his pieces have only come down to us thanks to the [[First Folio]] of 1623, published after his death.
He goes from laughter to blood. *Romeo and Juliet*, *Othello*, *King Lear*: families, power, jealousy. The “history plays” reenact England for an audience who likes to see themselves in epic form.
Comedies and tragedies respond to each other. The madman speaks the truth; the king goes mad. This porosity of tones explains why it can still be mounted in a thousand ways.

blocks.caption: The First Folio: saving texts from oblivion.

blocks.text: Translated, adapted, sampled by cinema and rap, Shakespeare remains a toolbox for expressing ambition and desire. His secret: writing for actors, in front of a crowd.
To fully understand Shakespeare's theater, you must keep one thing in mind: each technical detail serves an emotion or an idea. The work is never just decorative.
Context matters as much as style. Dates, places, sponsors, public: all this explains why a form appears at a specific moment, and not before.
Finally, legacy is measured over the long term. What we see today in museums, films or popular music still bears the traces of these inventions.
Translated in the 18th century in France and elsewhere, it became a world classic. Each era finds its mirror in him: romantic, political, postcolonial, feminist.
At the Globe, Shakespeare invented a popular theater whose characters and language conquered the world.
